To machinate means to secretly plot or scheme against someone, usually with the intention of causing them harm or gaining an unfair advantage over them.

It is not just any kind of planning. It is sneaky, calculated, and almost always done with bad intentions. Think of a villain sitting in the shadows, carefully working out a plan to destroy someone — that is machinating.

Three things are almost always true when someone machinates:

1. It is secret.
The person doing it does not want others — especially the target — to know what they are up to. It happens behind closed doors, in whispers, in hidden meetings.

2. It is deliberate and calculated.
This is not an impulsive action. Machinating involves careful, step-by-step planning. The schemer thinks things through, anticipates outcomes, and sets traps. There is a cold, crafty intelligence to it.

3. It is harmful or underhanded in purpose.
You do not machinate to do something good or neutral. The goal is almost always to bring someone down, to manipulate a situation to your benefit at someone else's expense, or to deceive people in a serious way. It carries a strong sense of moral wrongness.

Machinate is a heavy, dark word. It sounds exactly as sinister as it means. When you use it to describe someone's actions, you are painting them as devious, cold-blooded, and morally corrupt — not just "naughty" or "mischievous," but genuinely scheming and potentially dangerous.

It is a formal and somewhat literary word. You are unlikely to hear it in everyday casual conversation, but you will find it in serious writing, historical accounts, political commentary, and literature — especially when the writer wants to convey a sense of calculated, deep-seated treachery.
How It Differs from Similar Words

You might think: isn't this the same as "plot," "scheme," or "conspire"? They are all close in meaning, but machinate is the sharpest and most sinister of the group.

  • Plot — general planning toward a goal, not always negative. (They plotted a surprise party.)
  • Scheme — suggests cunning and self-interest, but can sometimes be used lightly. (He schemed his way to the top.)
  • Conspire — focuses on two or more people agreeing secretly to do something wrong. It emphasizes the group nature of the plan.
  • Machinate — the most loaded of all. It emphasizes the cold, elaborate, morally bankrupt nature of the planning itself. It almost always feels calculated and cruel, and it applies to both individuals and groups.

FormWordExample Use
VerbmachinateShe machinated against her rivals.
Present participlemachinatingHe spent years machinating in the background.
Noun (the act/plot itself)machination / machinationsHer machinations finally came to light.
Person who does itmachinatorHe was a ruthless machinator.

Note: Machinations (the plural noun) is actually the more commonly used form in everyday writing. You will often see phrases like "political machinations," "dark machinations," or "the machinations of the corrupt official." Getting comfortable with this noun form will help you recognise and use the word family well.

These examples show the word across different contexts so you can see how it behaves:

  1. The ambitious minister spent years machinating against the king, slowly turning the royal court against him.
  2. She refused to machinate behind her colleague's back, even when others pressured her to.
  3. It was later revealed that the board members had been machinating to force the founder out of his own company.
  4. A true leader does not need to machinate — they earn loyalty openly.
  5. He machinated carefully, placing his allies in key positions before making his move.

If you ever want to check whether a situation fits the word, ask yourself three quick questions:

  • Is it secret? ✓
  • Is it calculated and deliberate? ✓
  • Is it intended to harm or unfairly advantage someone? ✓

If all three are yes, machinate is the right word.

Machinate is a word that captures a very specific kind of human behaviour — the slow, quiet, deliberate work of someone who is building a trap in the dark. It goes beyond simple dishonesty into something more chilling: sustained, purposeful, hidden scheming. Whenever you encounter a character in a novel, a historical figure, or a real-world person who is described as machinatingRemove, you know you are dealing with someone who is not just bad, but strategically and coldly so.
